newsitem.title: JAPAN: More firms to fail as Japan economy falters - report.
newsitem.headline: More firms to fail as Japan economy falters - report.

text.p: Corporate Japan suffered a high rate of business failures last year, and more pain is in store as the economy struggles to achieve solid recovery, a research company said Tuesday.

Last year saw some of the biggest bankruptcies in the postwar period as companies sank under the weight of debts left over from the freewheeling "bubble" era of the 1980s, Tokyo Commerce and Industry Research Co. said in its report.

Total debts held by firms which went bust in 1996 declined 12.1 percent from the previous year to 8.12 trillion yen ($68.8 billion). But Tokyo Commerce said this was still the third-highest figure on record, showing the problem was still severe despite some improvement in the economy.
Total debt hit a record high of 9.24 trillion yen ($78.3 billion) in 1995.
The firm said the outlook was grim and predicted the number of bankruptcies would rise this year to more than 15,000, slightly above the 14,834 recorded in 1996.
"The number of bankruptcies induced by the economic slump continues to be at an alarming level, especially among small and medium-sized firms," it said.
It said there was a widening gap between the earnings of companies that were doing well and weaker firms.
The research firm said the lingering bad loan problem and changes in the economic structure would likely continue to induce a considerable number of failures this year.
It also cited concern about the effects on consumption of a rise in the sales tax April 1 to 5 percent from the current 3 percent.

The new year has already seen a raft of big failures, the latest being Kyotaru Co. Ltd., a major sushi chain listed on the first section of the Tokyo stock market, which failed earlier this week with debts of 101.3 billion yen ($858 million) from losses in investments and poor business.
Last October, Japan suffered its biggest postwar failure when loan firm Nichiei Finance Co. Ltd. folded with total debts of more than 1 trillion yen ($8.4 billion).
Another large failure was that of realtor Sueno Kosan, which collapsed with debts of about 716 billion yen ($6.06 billion). Sueno borrowed heavily from failed mortgage firms.
The number of failures fell in 1996, but only by 1.8 percent from 1995 despite a tentative recovery in the economy after years of post-bubble slump.
